statement: Similar cones and cylinders are to one another in the triplicate ratio of the diameters in their bases.
heath_proof: Let there be similar cones and cylinders, let the circles ABCD, EFGH be their bases, BD, FH the diameters of the bases, and KL, MN the axes of the cones and cylinders; I say that the cone of which the circle ABCD is the base and the point L the vertex has to the cone of which the circle EFGH is the base and the point N the vertex the ratio triplicate of that which BD has to FH. For, if the cone ABCDL has not to the cone EFGHN the ratio triplicate of that which BD has to FH, the cone ABCDL will have that triplicate ratio either to some solid less than the cone EFGHN or to a greater. First, let it have that triplicate ratio to a less solid O. Let the square EFGH be inscribed in the circle EFGH; [IV. 6] therefore the square EFGH is greater than the half of the circle EFGH. Now let there be set up on the square EFGH a pyramid having the same vertex with the cone; therefore the pyramid so set up is greater than the half part of the cone. Let the circumferences EF, FG, GH, HE be bisected at the points P, Q, R, S, and let EP, PF, FQ, QG, GR, RH, HS, SE be joined. Therefore each of the triangles EPF, FQG, GRH, HSE is also greater than the half part of that segment of the circle EFGH which is about it. Now on each of the triangles EPF, FQG, GRH, HSE let a pyramid be set up having the same vertex with the cone; therefore each of the pyramids so set up is also greater than the half part of that segment of the cone which is about it. Thus, bisecting the circumferences so left, joining straight lines, setting up on each of the triangles pyramids having the same vertex with the cone, and doing this continually, we shall leave some segments of the cone which will be less than the excess by which the cone EFGHN exceeds the solid O. [X. 1] Let such be left, and let them be the segments on EP, PF, FQ, QG, GR, RH, HS, SE; therefore the remainder, the pyramid of which the polygon EPFQGRHS is the base and the point N the vertex, is greater than the solid O. Let there be also inscribed in the circle ABCD the polygon ATBUCVDW similar and similarly situated to the polygon EPFQGRHS, and let there be set up on the polygon ATBUCVDW a pyramid having the same vertex with the cone; of the triangles containing the pyramid of which the polygon ATBUCVDW is the base and the point L the vertex let LBT be one, and of the triangles containing the pyramid of which the polygon EPFQGRHS is the base and the point N the vertex let NFP be one; and let KT, MP be joined. Now, since the cone ABCDL is similar to the cone EFGHN, therefore, as BD is to FH, so is the axis KL to the axis MN. [XI. Def. 24] But, as BD is to FH, so is BK to FM; therefore also, as BK is to FM, so is KL to MN. And, alternately, as BK is to KL, so is FM to MN. [V. 16] And the sides are proportional about equal angles, namely the angles BKL, FMN; therefore the triangle BKL is similar to the triangle FMN. [VI. 6] Again, since, as BK is to KT, so is FM to MP, and they are about equal angles, namely the angles BKT, FMP, inasmuch as, whatever part the angle BKT is of the four right angles at the centre K, the same part also is the angle FMP of the four right angles at the centre M; since then the sides are proportional about equal angles, therefore the triangle BKT is similar to the triangle FMP. [VI. 6] Again, since it was proved that, as BK is to KL, so is FM to MN, while BK is equal to KT, and FM to PM, therefore, as TK is to KL, so is PM to MN; and the sides are proportional about equal angles, namely the angles TKL, PMN, for they are right; therefore the triangle LKT is similar to the triangle NMP. [VI. 6] And since, owing to the similarity of the triangles LKB, NMF, as LB is to BK, so is NF to FM, and, owing to the similarity of the triangles BKT, FMP, as KB is to BT, so is MF to FP, therefore, ex aequali, as LB is to BT, so is NF to FP. [V. 22] Again since, owing to the similarity of the triangles LTK, NPM, as LT is to TK, so is NP to PM, and, owing to the similarity of the triangles TKB, PMF, as KT is to TB, so is MP to PF; therefore, ex aequali, as LT is to TB, so is NP to PF. [V. 22] But it was also proved that, as TB is to BL, so is PF to FN. Therefore, ex aequali, as TL is to LB, so is PN to NF. [V. 22] Therefore in the triangles LTB, NPF the sides are proportional; therefore the triangles LTB, NPF are equiangular; [VI. 5] hence they are also similar. [VI. Def. I] Therefore the pyramid of which the triangle BKT is the base and the point L the vertex is also similar to the pyramid of which the triangle FMP is the base and the point N the vertex, for they are contained by similar planes equal in multitude. [XI. Def. 9] But similar pyramids which have triangular bases are to one another in the triplicate ratio of their corresponding sides. [XII. 8] Therefore the pyramid BKTL has to the pyramid FMPN the ratio triplicate of that which BK has to FM. Similarly, by joining straight lines from A, W, D, V, C, U to K, and from E, S, H, R, G, Q to M, and setting up on each of the triangles pyramids which have the same vertex with the cones, we can prove that each of the similarly arranged pyramids will also have to each similarly arranged pyramid the ratio triplicate of that which the corresponding side BK has to the corresponding side FM, that is, which BD has to FH. And, as one of the antecedents is to one of the consequents, so are all the antecedents to all the consequents; [V. 12] therefore also, as the pyramid BKTL is to the pyramid FMPN, so is the whole pyramid of which the polygon ATBUCVDW is the base and the point L the vertex to the whole pyramid of which the polygon EPFQGRHS is the base and the point N the vertex; hence also the pyramid of which ATBUCVDW is the base and the point L the vertex has to the pyramid of which the polygon EPFQGRHS is the base and the point N the vertex the ratio triplicate of that which BD has to FH. But, by hypothesis, the cone of which the circle ABCD  is the base and the point L the vertex has also to the solid O the ratio triplicate of that which BD has to FH; therefore, as the cone of which the circle ABCD is the base and the point L the vertex is to the solid O, so is the pyramid of which the polygon ATBUCVDW is the base and L the vertex to the pyramid of which the polygon EPFQGRHS is the base and the point N the vertex; therefore, alternately, as the cone of which the circle ABCD is the base and L the vertex is to the pyramid contained in it of which the polygon ATBUCVDW is the base and L the vertex, so is the solid O to the pyramid of which the polygon EPFQGRHS is the base and N the vertex. [V. 16] But the said cone is greater than the pyramid in it; for it encloses it. Therefore the solid O is also greater than the pyramid of which the polygon EPFQGRHS is the base and N the vertex. But it is also less: which is impossible. Therefore the cone of which the circle ABCD is the base and L the vertex has not to any solid less than the cone of which the circle EFGH is the base and the point N the vertex the ratio triplicate of that which BD has to FH: Similarly we can prove that neither has the cone EFGHN to any solid less than the cone ABCDL the ratio triplicate of that which FH has to BD. I say next that neither has the cone ABCDL to any solid greater than the cone EFGHN the ratio triplicate of that which BD has to FH. For, if possible, let it have that ratio to a greater solid O. Therefore, inversely, the solid O has to the cone ABCDL the ratio triplicate of that which FH has to BD. But, as the solid O is to the cone ABCDL, so is the cone EFGHN to some solid less than the cone ABCDL. Therefore the cone EFGHN also has to some solid less than the cone ABCDL the ratio triplicate of that which FH has to BD: which was proved impossible. Therefore the cone ABCDL has not to any solid greater than the cone EFGHN the ratio triplicate of that which BD has to FH. But it was proved that neither has it this ratio to a less solid than the cone EFGHN. Therefore the cone ABCDL has to the cone EFGHN the ratio triplicate of that which BD has to FH. But, as the cone is to the cone, so is the cylinder to the cylinder, for the cylinder which is on the same base as the cone and of equal height with it is triple of the cone; [XII. 10] therefore the cylinder also has to the cylinder the ratio triplicate of that which BD has to FH.
ai_proof_text:
12.12
**Statement:** Similar cones and cylinders are to one another in the triplicate ratio of the diameters in their bases.

**Step 1.** Let there be similar cones whose bases are the circles ABCD, EFGH with centres K, M and diameters BD, FH, whose axes are KL, MN, and whose vertices are L, N; call them the cones ABCDL and EFGHN. Since the cones are similar, their axes and the diameters of their bases are proportional (D11.24): BD : FH = KL : MN. I say that the cone ABCDL has to the cone EFGHN the ratio triplicate of that which BD has to FH.

**Step 2.** Each cone is generated by a right-angled triangle turned about one of the sides containing the right angle; the side which remains fixed is the axis, and the other side about the right angle describes the base (D11.18, D11.19, D11.20). As the triangle turns, the moving side, which is always at right angles to the axis, takes the position of every radius of the base. Hence the axis KL is at right angles to every radius of the circle ABCD drawn from K, and MN to every radius of the circle EFGH drawn from M: the angles which KL makes with KA, KB, … and MN with ME, MF, … are right, and all these right angles are equal to one another (P4).

**Step 3.** Since K is the centre, KB = KD (D1.15), so that BD is double KB; likewise FH is double MF. Parts have the same ratio as the same multiples of them taken in corresponding order (5.15), so KB : MF = BD : FH. But BD : FH = KL : MN (Step 1); therefore KB : MF = KL : MN (5.11), and, alternately, KB : KL = MF : MN (5.16). Every radius KX of the circle ABCD is equal to KB and every radius MY of the circle EFGH is equal to MF (D1.15), so KX : KL = KB : KL and MY : MN = MF : MN (5.7); hence for any radii KX, MY we have KX : KL = MY : MN (5.11).

**Step 4.** Suppose that the cone ABCDL has not to the cone EFGHN the ratio triplicate of BD : FH. Then the cone ABCDL has that triplicate ratio to some solid O which is either less or greater than the cone EFGHN. First let O be less than the cone EFGHN.

**Step 5.** Inscribe in the circle EFGH the square EFGH (4.6) and circumscribe about the circle a square (4.7); by the construction of 4.7 each side of the circumscribed square is equal to the diameter FH, so the circumscribed square is the square on FH. In the inscribed square the angle FEH is right and EF = EH (D1.22), so the square on FH is equal to the squares on EF, EH together (1.47), that is, to double the square EFGH. Therefore the inscribed square EFGH is half of the circumscribed square.

**Step 6.** Set up on the square EFGH the pyramid with vertex N, and on the circumscribed square the pyramid with the same vertex N. These pyramids are of the same height, so they are to one another as their bases (12.6); hence the pyramid on the inscribed square is half of the pyramid on the circumscribed square. The circle EFGH lies within the circumscribed square, so the cone EFGHN is a part of the pyramid on the circumscribed square with vertex N and is less than it (CN5). Therefore the pyramid on the square EFGH with vertex N is greater than half of the cone EFGHN.

**Step 7.** Bisect the circumferences EF, FG, GH, HE at P, Q, R, S (3.30) and join EP, PF, FQ, QG, GR, RH, HS, SE (P1). Consider the triangle EPF and the segment of the circle on EF which contains it. In the construction of 3.30, P lies on the straight line drawn at right angles to EF from its middle point; this line passes through the centre M (3.1, porism), so MP is at right angles to EF. Draw through P a straight line at right angles to MP (1.11); it touches the circle at P and otherwise lies outside the circle (3.16, porism). Since EF and this tangent are both at right angles to MP, they are parallel (1.28). Draw through E and F straight lines parallel to MP (1.31) meeting the tangent at E′, F′; then EFF′E′ is a parallelogram on the base EF, and the triangle EPF, being on the same base EF and between the same parallels EF, E′F′, is half of the parallelogram EFF′E′ (1.41). The segment of the circle on EF is a part of the parallelogram EFF′E′ and so is less than it (CN5). Therefore the triangle EPF is greater than half of the segment of the circle on EF; the same holds for the triangles FQG, GRH, HSE and the segments on FG, GH, HE.

**Step 8.** Set up on the triangle EPF the pyramid with vertex N, and on the parallelogram EFF′E′ the pyramid with vertex N. Being of the same height, they are to one another as their bases (12.6), so by Step 7 the pyramid on the triangle EPF is half of the pyramid on the parallelogram. The segment of the cone EFGHN standing on the segment of the circle on EF (the part of the cone cut off by the plane through N, E, F) is a part of the pyramid on the parallelogram EFF′E′ with vertex N, and so is less than it (CN5). Therefore the pyramid on EPF with vertex N is greater than half of the segment of the cone in which it stands; and likewise for the pyramids on FQG, GRH, HSE with vertex N.

**Step 9.** The cone EFGHN exceeds the solid O, and the excess is less than the cone (CN5). From the cone EFGHN subtract the pyramid on the square EFGH with vertex N, which is greater than its half (Step 6); there remain the four segments of the cone on EF, FG, GH, HE. From these subtract the pyramids on EPF, FQG, GRH, HSE with vertex N, each greater than half of the segment in which it stands (Step 8); there remain the segments of the cone on EP, PF, FQ, QG, GR, RH, HS, SE. Bisecting the remaining circumferences and continuing in the same way, we subtract at each stage more than half of what is left, so that by 10.1 we shall at some stage leave segments of the cone EFGHN which together are less than the excess of the cone EFGHN over O. For definiteness let this happen at the stage just reached, the remaining segments being those on EP, PF, FQ, QG, GR, RH, HS, SE (the argument is identical at any later stage). Let Π′ denote the pyramid with base the polygon EPFQGRHS and vertex N. The cone EFGHN is composed of Π′ together with these segments, and the segments are less than the excess of the cone over O; therefore Π′ is greater than O.

**Step 10.** In the circle ABCD inscribe the square ABCD (4.6) and bisect the circumferences AB, BC, CD, DA at T, U, V, W (3.30), so obtaining the polygon ATBUCVDW in the same manner as EPFQGRHS was obtained; join its sides (P1) and let Π denote the pyramid with base ATBUCVDW and vertex L. Join KA, KT, KB, KU, KC, KV, KD, KW and LA, LT, LB, LU, LC, LV, LD, LW, and likewise ME, MP, MF, MQ, MG, MR, MH, MS and NE, NP, NF, NQ, NG, NR, NH, NS (P1). The straight lines from K divide the polygon ATBUCVDW into the eight triangles KAT, KTB, KBU, KUC, KCV, KVD, KDW, KWA, and the planes through L and these lines divide Π into the eight pyramids on these triangles with vertex L; similarly Π′ is divided into the eight pyramids on MEP, MPF, MFQ, MQG, MGR, MRH, MHS, MSE with vertex N. Denote by KAT·L the pyramid with base KAT and vertex L, and similarly for the others. Consider the pair KAT·L, MEP·N; the first is contained by the four triangles KAT, KTL, KAL, ATL, the second by the four triangles MEP, MPN, MEN, EPN.

**Step 11.** By Step 3, KT : KL = MP : MN, and the angles TKL, PMN contained by these sides are right and hence equal (Step 2). Two triangles which have one angle equal to one angle and the sides about the equal angles proportional are equiangular, with the equal angles subtended by the corresponding sides (6.6); so the triangles KTL, MPN are equiangular and therefore similar (D6.1). In the same way, from KA : KL = ME : MN (Step 3) and the right angles AKL, EMN, the triangles KAL, MEN are equiangular and similar (6.6, D6.1).

**Step 12.** In the construction of 4.6 the square ABCD is inscribed by means of two diameters AC, BD at right angles, so the angle AKB is right. T bisects the circumference AB (Step 10), and angles at the centre standing on equal circumferences are equal (3.27), so the angle AKT is equal to the angle TKB and is half of the right angle AKB. Likewise the angle EMP is half of the right angle EMF. All right angles being equal (P4), their halves are equal: angle AKT = angle EMP. (In general, whatever part the angle AKT is of the four right angles at K, the same part is the angle EMP of the four right angles at M, both polygons arising from a square by the same number of bisections.) Moreover KA = KT and ME = MP (D1.15), so KA : KT = ME : MP, each being the ratio of a magnitude to a magnitude equal to it (D5.5). Hence, by 6.6, the triangles KAT, MEP are equiangular and similar (D6.1).

**Step 13.** From the similar triangles KTL, MPN we have LT : TK = NP : PM, and from the similar triangles KAT, MEP we have TK : TA = PM : PE (6.4); therefore, ex aequali, LT : TA = NP : PE (5.22). Again, from the similar triangles KAL, MEN, LA : AK = NE : EM, and from KAT, MEP, AK : AT = EM : EP (6.4); therefore, ex aequali, LA : AT = NE : EP (5.22). Taking these two proportions alternately (5.16), LT : NP = TA : PE and LA : NE = AT : EP; hence LT : NP = TA : PE = LA : NE (5.11). The triangles ATL, EPN thus have their sides proportional, so they are equiangular, the equal angles being subtended by the corresponding sides (6.5), and they are similar (D6.1).

**Step 14.** The pyramid KAT·L is therefore contained by four triangles KAT, KTL, KAL, ATL respectively similar to the four triangles MEP, MPN, MEN, EPN which contain the pyramid MEP·N; the two pyramids are contained by similar planes equal in multitude, and so are similar solid figures (D11.9). Similar pyramids which have triangular bases are to one another in the triplicate ratio of their corresponding sides (12.8); hence the pyramid KAT·L has to the pyramid MEP·N the ratio triplicate of that which KT has to MP. Now KT = KB and MP = MF (D1.15), so KT : MP = KB : MP = KB : MF (5.7), and KB : MF = BD : FH (Step 3); thus KT : MP = BD : FH (5.11), and the ratio triplicate of KT : MP is the ratio triplicate of BD : FH (D5.10). Therefore the pyramid KAT·L has to the pyramid MEP·N the ratio triplicate of BD : FH.

**Step 15.** In exactly the same way each of the remaining pyramids KTB·L, KBU·L, KUC·L, KCV·L, KVD·L, KDW·L, KWA·L has to the corresponding pyramid MPF·N, MFQ·N, MQG·N, MGR·N, MRH·N, MHS·N, MSE·N the ratio triplicate of BD : FH. These eight pairs are all in the same ratio; hence, as one of the antecedents is to its consequent, so are all the antecedents together to all the consequents together (5.12): Π : Π′ = pyramid KAT·L : pyramid MEP·N, that is, Π has to Π′ the ratio triplicate of BD : FH.

**Step 16.** By hypothesis the cone ABCDL has to O the ratio triplicate of BD : FH; therefore cone ABCDL : O = Π : Π′ (5.11). The pyramid Π has its vertex at L and its base within the circle ABCD, so it is a part of the cone ABCDL, and the cone ABCDL is greater than Π (CN5). In the proportion cone ABCDL : O = Π : Π′ the first magnitude is greater than the third, so the second is greater than the fourth (5.14): O is greater than Π′. But Π′ is greater than O (Step 9), which is impossible. Therefore the cone ABCDL has not to any solid less than the cone EFGHN the ratio triplicate of BD : FH.

**Step 17.** Interchanging the roles of the two cones throughout Steps 4–16, we see in the same way that the cone EFGHN has not to any solid less than the cone ABCDL the ratio triplicate of FH : BD.

**Step 18.** Next let O be greater than the cone EFGHN, the cone ABCDL having to O the ratio triplicate of BD : FH. Take X, Y such that BD : FH = FH : X = X : Y; then cone ABCDL : O = BD : Y (D5.10). Inversely (5.7, porism; D5.13), O : cone ABCDL = Y : BD, while Y : X = X : FH = FH : BD, so that Y : BD is the ratio triplicate of FH : BD (D5.10); thus O has to the cone ABCDL the ratio triplicate of FH : BD. Now let T be a solid such that O : cone ABCDL = cone EFGHN : T (the fourth proportional, assumed to exist as in Step 4). Since O is greater than the cone EFGHN, the first magnitude in this proportion is greater than the third, so the second is greater than the fourth (5.14): the cone ABCDL is greater than T. Thus cone EFGHN : T = O : cone ABCDL, which is the ratio triplicate of FH : BD (5.11), where T is a solid less than the cone ABCDL. This contradicts Step 17. Therefore the cone ABCDL has not to any solid greater than the cone EFGHN the ratio triplicate of BD : FH.

**Step 19.** The solid O to which the cone ABCDL has the ratio triplicate of BD : FH is thus neither less nor greater than the cone EFGHN; hence it is equal to it, and cone ABCDL : cone EFGHN = cone ABCDL : O (5.7), which is the ratio triplicate of BD : FH. Therefore similar cones are to one another in the triplicate ratio of the diameters of their bases.

**Step 20.** Now let there be similar cylinders whose bases are the circles ABCD, EFGH with diameters BD, FH and whose axes are KL, MN (D11.21, D11.22, D11.23), so that BD : FH = KL : MN (D11.24). The cones ABCDL, EFGHN which have the same bases and the same axes (generated by the right-angled triangles KBL, MFN turned about KL, MN) have their axes and diameters in the same proportion and so are similar cones (D11.24); by Step 19, cone ABCDL : cone EFGHN is the ratio triplicate of BD : FH. Each cylinder is triple of the cone which has the same base with it and equal height (12.10). Equimultiples have the same ratio as the magnitudes themselves (5.15); therefore cylinder ABCD·KL : cylinder EFGH·MN = cone ABCDL : cone EFGHN, which is the ratio triplicate of BD : FH.

**Step 21.** Therefore similar cones and cylinders are to one another in the triplicate ratio of the diameters in their bases. Q.E.D.
